cards.q: What are the two ways of representing the structure of benzene, and which is the accepted model?
cards.a: The Kekulé structure (a ring of alternating \(\mathrm{C{-}C}\) and \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bonds) and the delocalised model (a hexagon with a circle). The delocalised model is accepted.

answerFigure.alt: Two models of benzene side by side: on the left the Kekulé structure, a hexagon with alternating single and double bonds; on the right the delocalised model, a hexagon with a circle inside.

cards.why: The circle stands for six electrons shared over all six carbon atoms, not three separate double bonds.

cards.q: Describe the bonding in benzene in terms of orbitals.
cards.a: Each carbon’s spare p electron overlaps sideways with its neighbours’ to form a ring of delocalised π electrons.
marks: Each carbon forms three \(\sigma\) bonds: to two carbons and one hydrogen.
Each carbon has one electron left in a p orbital at right angles to the plane of the ring.
The p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring.
This forms a ring of delocalised \(\pi\) electron density above and below the plane, holding six electrons.

cards.q: Describe the shape of a benzene molecule.
cards.a: Planar, a regular hexagon: all six \(\mathrm{C{-}C}\) bonds are the same length and every bond angle is \(120^{\circ}\).

figure.alt: Benzene drawn as a regular hexagon with a circle inside, and a hydrogen atom bonded outwards from each of the six corners.

cards.why: Each carbon has three bonding regions and no lone pairs, so it is trigonal planar.

cards.q: The \(\mathrm{C{-}C}\) bond length is 0.154 nm and the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bond length is 0.134 nm. Every carbon–carbon bond in benzene is 0.139 nm. Explain how this supports the delocalised model.
cards.a: All the bonds are the same length, between a single and a double bond.
marks: The Kekulé structure would have two different bond lengths: three short and three long.
X-ray diffraction shows all six bonds are identical.
Their length is intermediate between single and double, because the π electrons are shared equally round the ring.

cards.q: What is the enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene, and what does it suggest for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
cards.a: \(\Delta H = -120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) for one \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\). A molecule with three \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bonds would be expected to give \(3 \times (-120) = -360\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

answerFigure.alt: Cyclohexene reacts with hydrogen, with a nickel catalyst, to form cyclohexane.

cards.why: Cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is the theoretical Kekulé molecule.

cards.q: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is \(-120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); that of benzene is \(-208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). How much more stable is benzene than cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
cards.a: \(152\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) more stable

figure.alt: Benzene reacts with three moles of hydrogen, with a nickel catalyst, to form cyclohexane.

cards.why: Less energy is released because benzene starts lower in energy: the delocalisation energy.

cards.q: Use enthalpies of hydrogenation to explain why benzene is more stable than the theoretical molecule cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
cards.a: Less energy is released when benzene is hydrogenated than expected, so benzene is lower in energy.
marks: Hydrogenating one \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) releases \(120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), so three would release \(360\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Benzene releases only \(208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Both reactions give cyclohexane, so benzene is \(152\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) lower in energy (more stable).
The extra stability comes from the delocalisation of the p electrons.

cards.q: Give the evidence that the Kekulé structure does not describe benzene correctly.
cards.a: Bond lengths, enthalpy of hydrogenation and reactivity all disagree with three separate double bonds.
marks: All six carbon–carbon bonds are the same length, between single and double.
The enthalpy change of hydrogenation is much less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene.
Benzene does not decolourise bromine water and does not readily undergo addition, unlike alkenes.

cards.q: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions.
cards.a: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring; addition would destroy it.
marks: Addition would break up the delocalised π system.
The product would lose the delocalisation stability (about \(152\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)).
In substitution a hydrogen is replaced, so the delocalised ring is restored in the product.

cards.q: Explain why cyclohexene decolourises bromine water at room temperature but benzene does not.
cards.a: The π electrons in an alkene are localised; in benzene they are spread over the whole ring.
marks: In cyclohexene the \(\pi\) electrons are localised between two carbon atoms: a region of high electron density.
This can induce a dipole in \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\), which is then attacked.
In benzene the \(\pi\) electrons are delocalised over six carbons, so the electron density is lower.
It cannot polarise \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) enough, so a catalyst is needed to make a stronger electrophile.

cards.q: True or false: benzene has three single and three double bonds that keep switching places.
cards.a: False. All six bonds are identical at all times: six π electrons are delocalised round the whole ring.
cards.why: Benzene is not two Kekulé structures flicking between each other; it is one structure, more stable than either.

cards.q: Write the equation for the complete combustion of benzene, and describe its flame.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{6} + 7\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 6CO_{2} + 3H_{2}O}\)
It burns with a very smoky (sooty) flame.
cards.why: Benzene has a high carbon to hydrogen ratio, so in air much of the carbon burns incompletely, forming soot.

cards.q: What is an electrophile, and why is benzene attacked by electrophiles?
cards.a: An electron pair acceptor. Benzene’s ring of delocalised π electrons is a region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles.
cards.why: Electrophiles are positive ions or the δ+ end of a polarised molecule.

cards.q: Give the reagents and conditions for the nitration of benzene, and name the product.
cards.a: Concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, at about \(50\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\) (below \(55\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\)). Product: nitrobenzene.

answerFigure.alt: Benzene reacts with nitric acid, catalysed by sulfuric acid at 50 °C, to give nitrobenzene and water.

cards.why: The sulfuric acid is a catalyst: it is used to make the electrophile and is regenerated.

cards.q: Write an equation for the formation of the nitronium ion from concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids.
cards.why: Also accepted: \(\mathrm{HNO_{3} + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow NO_{2}^{+} + HSO_{4}^{-} + H_{2}O}\). Sulfuric acid is the stronger acid and protonates nitric acid.

cards.q: Show how the sulfuric acid catalyst is regenerated in the nitration of benzene.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H^{+} + HSO_{4}^{-} \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{4}}\)
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) lost from the ring in the last step combines with the hydrogensulfate ion.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the nitration of benzene.
cards.a: Electrophilic substitution: the ring attacks \(\mathrm{NO_{2}^{+}}\); the intermediate loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to restore the delocalised ring.

answerFigure.alt: Nitration mechanism. A curly arrow from the delocalised ring to the N of the nitronium ion. In the positive intermediate the top carbon carries H and NO2 and a horseshoe covers the other five carbons. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring gives nitrobenzene and H+.

cards.why: The arrow starts at the circle and goes to the N; the horseshoe in the intermediate must not cover the carbon that carries the H and the NO₂.

cards.q: Why is the temperature kept below \(55\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\) when benzene is nitrated?
cards.a: To prevent further substitution.
marks: At higher temperatures more than one nitro group substitutes onto the ring.
Keeping the temperature low gives mainly the monosubstituted product, nitrobenzene.

cards.q: Give two reasons why nitration is an important step in synthesis.
cards.a: It is used to make explosives, such as TNT, and nitro compounds are reduced to aromatic amines, which are used to make dyes.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of TNT, 2-methyl-1,3,5-trinitrobenzene: a methylbenzene ring with three nitro groups.

cards.why: The figure shows TNT, made by nitrating methylbenzene three times.

cards.q: 7.80 g of benzene (\(M_{\text{r}} = 78.0\)) is nitrated, giving 9.84 g of nitrobenzene (\(M_{\text{r}} = 123.0\)). Calculate the percentage yield.
cards.a: 80.0%
steps: Moles of benzene \(= \frac{7.80}{78.0} = 0.100\ \text{mol}\), so 0.100 mol of nitrobenzene is possible.
cards.why: One mole of benzene gives one mole of nitrobenzene.

cards.q: Methyl 3-nitrobenzoate is made by nitrating methyl benzoate. Describe how the crude solid is purified by recrystallisation.
cards.a: Dissolve in the minimum of hot solvent, filter hot, cool to crystallise, filter under reduced pressure, wash with a little cold solvent, dry.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of methyl 3-nitrobenzoate: a benzene ring with a CO2CH3 ester group and a nitro group on the carbon two along from it.

cards.why: Soluble impurities stay in the cold solution; insoluble ones are removed by the hot filtration.

cards.q: How does a melting point show whether a sample of methyl 3-nitrobenzoate is pure?
cards.a: A pure sample melts sharply, over a narrow range, at the data-book value. Impurities lower the melting point and widen the range.
cards.why: Compare the measured value with the data-book value for the compound.

cards.q: Give the reagents and conditions for the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride, and name the product.
cards.a: Ethanoyl chloride with an aluminium chloride catalyst, heated under reflux in dry conditions. Product: phenylethanone (and \(\mathrm{HCl}\)).

answerFigure.alt: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride, with aluminium chloride catalyst under reflux, to give phenylethanone and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: Acylation forms a new carbon–carbon bond, making an aromatic ketone.

cards.q: Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile when ethanoyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + AlCl_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CO^{+} + AlCl_{4}^{-}}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) is a Lewis acid: it accepts a lone pair from the chlorine of the acyl chloride.

cards.q: Show how the aluminium chloride catalyst is regenerated in Friedel–Crafts acylation.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H^{+} + AlCl_{4}^{-} \rightarrow AlCl_{3} + HCl}\)
cards.why: This is why \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a product of the overall reaction.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of benzene with the acylium ion, CH₃CO⁺.
cards.a: Electrophilic substitution: the ring attacks the positive carbon of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO^{+}}\); the intermediate loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).

answerFigure.alt: Acylation mechanism. A curly arrow from the delocalised ring to the positive carbon of the acylium ion, CH3–C+=O. In the positive intermediate the top carbon carries H and COCH3. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring gives phenylethanone and H+.

cards.why: The arrow must go to the carbon of the acylium ion, which carries the positive charge, not to the oxygen.

cards.q: Why must the aluminium chloride and the apparatus be dry in Friedel–Crafts reactions?
cards.a: Water reacts with aluminium chloride.
marks: \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) is hydrolysed by water (giving \(\mathrm{HCl}\) fumes).
It would no longer act as a catalyst, so the electrophile would not form.

cards.q: Benzene is heated under reflux with propanoyl chloride and aluminium chloride. Name the organic product.
cards.a: 1-phenylpropan-1-one

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 1-phenylpropan-1-one: a benzene ring bonded to a C=O carbon that carries an ethyl group.

steps: It replaces one H on the ring: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}COCH_{2}CH_{3}}\).
A three-carbon ketone chain with the C=O on carbon 1, bonded to a phenyl group.
cards.why: The other product is \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

cards.q: Why are Friedel–Crafts acylation reactions important in synthesis?
cards.a: They form a new carbon–carbon bond to the ring, giving aromatic ketones that can be converted into other compounds.
cards.why: For example, the ketone can be reduced to a secondary alcohol. A Friedel–Crafts acylation is a step in one industrial route to ibuprofen.

cards.q: Give the reagents and conditions for the bromination of benzene, and name the product.
cards.a: Bromine with a halogen carrier catalyst such as \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\) (or iron filings), at room temperature. Product: bromobenzene and \(\mathrm{HBr}\).

answerFigure.alt: Benzene reacts with bromine, with iron(III) bromide catalyst, to give bromobenzene and hydrogen bromide.

cards.why: Iron filings react with bromine to make \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\), the real catalyst.

cards.q: Write equations to show how \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\) forms the electrophile for bromination, and how it is regenerated.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Br_{2} + FeBr_{3} \rightarrow Br^{+} + FeBr_{4}^{-}}\)
\(\mathrm{H^{+} + FeBr_{4}^{-} \rightarrow FeBr_{3} + HBr}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\) accepts a lone pair from one bromine atom, polarising and breaking the \(\mathrm{Br{-}Br}\) bond.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the bromination of benzene with \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\).
cards.a: Electrophilic substitution: the ring attacks the \(\delta+\) bromine, the \(\mathrm{Br{-}Br}\) bond breaks, and the intermediate loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).

answerFigure.alt: Bromination mechanism. Br–Br is polarised by FeBr3. A curly arrow from the ring to the δ+ bromine, and from the Br–Br bond to the δ− bromine. In the positive intermediate the top carbon carries H and Br. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring gives bromobenzene and H+.

cards.why: Starting from \(\mathrm{Br^{+}}\), with the \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\) step shown separately, is also accepted.

cards.q: Give the reagents and conditions for the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene to make methylbenzene.
cards.a: Chloromethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heated under reflux. Products: methylbenzene and \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

answerFigure.alt: Benzene reacts with chloromethane, with aluminium chloride catalyst, to give methylbenzene and hydrogen chloride.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl + AlCl_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}^{+} + AlCl_{4}^{-}}\)

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of benzene with the methyl carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}^{+}}\).
cards.a: Electrophilic substitution: the ring attacks \(\mathrm{CH_{3}^{+}}\); the intermediate loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to give methylbenzene.

answerFigure.alt: Alkylation mechanism. A curly arrow from the delocalised ring to the carbon of the CH3+ ion. In the positive intermediate the top carbon carries H and CH3. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring gives methylbenzene and H+.

cards.why: The \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{AlCl_{4}^{-}}\), regenerating \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) and forming \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

cards.q: Why are \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{FeBr_{3}}\) called halogen carriers?
cards.a: Each accepts a lone pair from a halogen atom of the reagent and takes it as a halide ion (forming \(\mathrm{AlCl_{4}^{-}}\) or \(\mathrm{FeBr_{4}^{-}}\)), leaving a positive electrophile. The halide is handed back when the catalyst is regenerated.
cards.why: Al in \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) has only six outer electrons, so it is a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor).

cards.q: What do the electrophilic substitution reactions of benzene have in common?
cards.a: A strong electrophile is made first; the ring attacks it to form a positive intermediate; the intermediate loses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to restore the delocalised ring; the catalyst is regenerated.
cards.why: Nitration: \(\mathrm{NO_{2}^{+}}\). Acylation: \(\mathrm{RCO^{+}}\). Edexcel also: \(\mathrm{Br^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{R^{+}}\).

cards.q: True or false: in the intermediate of electrophilic substitution, the horseshoe of delocalised electrons is drawn over all six carbon atoms.
cards.a: False. It covers only five carbons. The carbon carrying both the H and the new group is sp³ and is left out of the horseshoe.
cards.why: The + charge is drawn inside the horseshoe: the positive charge is spread over the five carbons.

cards.q: True or false: in electrophilic substitution, the benzene ring loses a hydride ion, H⁻.
cards.a: False. It loses a proton, \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).
cards.why: The two electrons of the C–H bond go back into the ring to restore the delocalised system.

cards.q: Describe what you see when bromine water is added to phenol, and name the product.
cards.a: The orange bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate forms: 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

answerFigure.alt: Phenol reacts with three moles of bromine water at room temperature to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}OH + 3Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{6}H_{2}Br_{3}OH + 3HBr}\). No catalyst is needed.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of phenol with bromine water.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}OH + 3Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{6}H_{2}Br_{3}OH + 3HBr}\)

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenol: a benzene ring with an OH group attached.

cards.why: Three hydrogens on the ring are substituted, at positions 2, 4 and 6.

cards.q: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine much more readily than benzene does.
cards.a: A lone pair on the oxygen is partly delocalised into the ring, increasing its electron density.
marks: A lone pair in a p orbital on the oxygen overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring.
This increases the electron density of the ring.
The ring can now polarise \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) molecules itself, so no halogen carrier catalyst is needed.
The ring is attacked more readily, and three bromine atoms substitute.

cards.q: Name this compound, formed when phenol reacts with bromine water.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: a phenol ring with bromine atoms on both carbons next to the OH and on the carbon opposite it.

cards.a: 2,4,6-tribromophenol
cards.why: Number round the ring from the carbon carrying the OH group (carbon 1).

cards.q: Name this compound, the product of the nitration of benzene.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of nitrobenzene: a benzene ring with an NO2 group attached.

cards.a: Nitrobenzene
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{-NO_{2}}\) group is named with the prefix nitro-.

cards.q: Name this compound, the product of the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylethanone: a benzene ring bonded to a C=O carbon that carries a methyl group.

cards.a: Phenylethanone
cards.why: A two-carbon ketone (ethanone) with a phenyl group, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}}\), on the carbonyl carbon.

cards.q: Name this compound, the product of the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene with chloromethane.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of methylbenzene: a benzene ring with one methyl group.

cards.a: Methylbenzene
cards.why: Methylbenzene (toluene) is often used in place of benzene in school laboratories because benzene is carcinogenic.

cards.q: What is a phenyl group?
cards.a: A benzene ring that has lost one hydrogen atom, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}{-}}\), bonded to the rest of a molecule.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylmethanol: a benzene ring bonded to a CH2OH group.

cards.why: The compound shown is phenylmethanol: a phenyl group on methanol.

cards.q: Draw the product of the nitration of methyl benzoate, methyl 3-nitrobenzoate.
cards.a: A benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{-COOCH_{3}}\) on carbon 1 and \(\mathrm{-NO_{2}}\) on carbon 3.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of methyl 3-nitrobenzoate: a benzene ring with a CO2CH3 ester group and a nitro group on the carbon two along from it.

cards.why: The ester group directs the incoming nitro group to position 3.

cards.q: Why does it not matter which carbon of benzene is attacked in a monosubstitution?
cards.a: All six carbon atoms are equivalent, so there is only one possible monosubstituted product.

figure.alt: Benzene drawn as a regular hexagon with a circle inside, and a hydrogen atom bonded outwards from each of the six corners.

cards.why: There is only one nitrobenzene, one bromobenzene and one phenylethanone.

cards.q: Give a two-step route from benzene to phenylamine.
cards.a:
1. Nitration: conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_{3}}\) and conc. \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\), \(50\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\), giving nitrobenzene.
2. Reduction: tin and conc. \(\mathrm{HCl}\), heat under reflux, then \(\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}\).

answerFigure.alt: Nitrobenzene is reduced by tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid to phenylamine and water.

cards.q: Why is the intermediate in electrophilic substitution less stable than benzene?
cards.a: Its delocalised system is partly broken: only four π electrons are spread over five carbons, and one carbon is sp³ with four single bonds.
cards.why: Losing \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) restores the full delocalised ring, so the reaction ends in substitution.
